item.title: Exploring Non-Standard Data Types: Systems with CHAR_BIT Not Equal to 8 and Non-IEEE Floating Point
item.description:
“Exploring Non-Standard Data Types: Systems with CHAR_BIT Not Equal to 8 and Non-IEEE Floating Point”

Deviations in Data Representation Across Architectures

Several established and specialized architectures maintain data representation methods that challenge typical modern expectations.

Unisys ClearPath Dorado Servers and the 2200 Architecture

The Unisys ClearPath Dorado servers, designed to offer backward compatibility for older Univac software, exhibit several distinct characteristics:

  • Word Size: They operate using 36-bit words.
  • Character Size: Crucially, CHAR_BIT is defined as 9 bits.
  • Integer Representation: The architecture employs one’s complement for signed numbers.
  • Floating Point: They feature a 72-bit non-IEEE floating-point format.
  • Memory Model: There is a separation between the address space reserved for code and that for data.
  • Addressing: The system is word-addressed, and it notably lacks a dedicated stack pointer register.

Documentation, such as the referenced Unisys C Compiler Programming Reference Manual (Section 4.5), details data types utilizing 9, 18, 36, and 72 bits. While compiler availability (like C++) isn’t explicitly confirmed, the base architecture dictates these unusual specifications.

item.title: Optimizing Code Performance Through CPU Cache Utilization Strategies
item.description:
“Optimizing Code Performance Through CPU Cache Utilization Strategies”

The modern computational landscape is heavily constrained not by processor frequency, but by memory access latency. While registers offer immediate access, they are scarce. Main memory (DRAM) is vast but slow, requiring hundreds of clock cycles for data retrieval. Bridging this chasm are L1, L2, and L3 caches—hierarchical storage that balances speed and cost. Understanding and exploiting this hierarchy is paramount for writing truly fast code.

item.title: x64 Calling Conventions: UN*X vs. Windows Argument Register Differences Explained
item.description:
“x64 Calling Conventions: UN*X vs. Windows Argument Register Differences Explained”

When developing for x64 architectures, particularly when delving into low-level programming or compiler optimizations, the differences between the UN*X (System V AMD64 ABI) and Windows x64 calling conventions are significant. These conventions dictate how functions pass arguments and receive return values, directly impacting code efficiency and interoperability. Let’s break down these distinctions and the rationale behind them.

Argument Passing: Register Allocation

A primary difference lies in the number and specific assignment of registers used for passing function arguments.
